outline.description: Sets out the legal backdrop necessary to understand the dispute, focusing on the Office of Special Counsel’s authority under the Civil Service Reform Act and FOIA’s separate disciplinary mechanism.
subtopics: Role of the Office of Special Counsel (OSC) as an investigative/prosecutorial body for civil service integrity
Corrective and disciplinary pathways: 5 U.S.C. § 1214 (corrective action) and § 1215 (disciplinary action)
OSC’s authority to investigate non–personnel-practice misconduct under 5 U.S.C. § 1216, including § 1216(a)(3) on arbitrary or capricious FOIA withholding
Relationship between § 1216 and the procedures in § 1214 (notice provisions for prohibited personnel practice investigations)

FOIA’s distinct disciplinary trigger in 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(F)(i): three predicates (court-ordered production, fee award, and a judicial finding questioning arbitrary/capricious withholding) and the mandate that OSC promptly initiate a proceeding
Tension framed in the case: whether § 1216 investigations depend on satisfaction of FOIA § 552(a)(4)(F)(i), and whether § 1216 investigations import § 1214’s notice procedures

outline.description: Recounts AFL’s FOIA request, OSC petition, district court rulings, and posture on appeal to the D.C. Circuit.
subtopics: AFL’s FOIA request to DOJ for emails and DOJ Civil Division’s asserted policy not to search employee emails without consent
Parallel FOIA litigation against DOJ: ongoing production; adequacy not at issue in this appeal
AFL’s OSC complaint invoking § 1216(a)(3) to investigate an alleged DOJ FOIA-search policy
OSC’s initial refusal to investigate, premised on lack of FOIA § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) predicates

District court’s mixed rulings: held § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) does not limit § 1216 authority; deemed OSC’s legal premise erroneous; nonetheless declined to compel an investigation as discretionary under § 1216(c); remand to OSC
OSC’s renewed declination; district court’s final dismissal on the merits; AFL’s appeal; standard of review de novo
D.C. Circuit’s threshold inquiry into Article III standing and order for supplemental briefing on standing

outline.chapter_title: Article III Standing and the Procedural-Injury Framework
outline.description: Explains the constitutional standing requirements and how procedural-rights claims can relax but not eliminate certain elements.
subtopics: Core elements: injury in fact, causation, and redressability (Lujan; Allen v. Wright; Steel Co.)
Injury must be concrete, particularized, and actual or imminent; procedural rights in vacuo are insufficient (Summers v. Earth Island Institute)
Relaxed standing for procedural injuries: what is relaxed (imminence, some aspects of redressability) and what is not (injury in fact, causation) (Center for Law & Education; Florida Audubon)
Informational standing: entitlement-based model—concrete injury arises only when a statute grants a right to receive information (Akins; Public Citizen; ASPCA v. Feld; Zivotofsky)

Application to AFL’s framing: claimed procedural right to a § 1216 investigation and two asserted concrete interests (FOIA records from DOJ; notices/information from an OSC investigation under § 1214)

outline.chapter_title: AFL’s First Theory: Denial of FOIA Records and the Causation/Redressability Gap
outline.description: Analyzes why OSC’s refusal to investigate cannot ground standing based on AFL’s non-receipt of DOJ records requested under FOIA.
subtopics: Traceability problem: informational injury from nondisclosure is attributable to DOJ, not OSC
Speculative causal chain: OSC investigation → OSC enforcement choice under §§ 1214/1215 → MSPB sanctions → DOJ changes production practices → AFL receives records

Independent-actor barrier: reliance on discretionary decisions of non-parties (MSPB and DOJ) defeats causation (FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine; Haaland v. Brackeen on redressability focusing on parties before the court)
Agency enforcement discretion: courts generally may not compel how OSC exercises prosecutorial discretion (Heckler v. Chaney)

Redressability shortfall: a favorable judgment would not very likely spur the necessary subsequent steps (Hecate Energy v. FERC); judgments bind parties, not third-party agencies likely to make independent choices
Conclusion: no standing on the FOIA-records theory due to speculative, attenuated causation and lack of likely redressability

outline.chapter_title: AFL’s Second Theory: Informational Injury from OSC Investigation Processes and the Absence of Entitlement
outline.description: Explains why AFL’s claim to investigation-related notices and updates fails to establish informational standing and why redressability remains deficient.
subtopics: Entitlement prerequisite: informational standing requires a statutory right to receive information
Section 1216(a)(3) obligation to investigate, even if mandatory, does not itself confer a right to receive information

AFL’s reliance on § 1214 notice provisions: those procedures apply to prohibited-personnel-practice investigations and are discretionary, not mandatory, in § 1216 investigations (Carson v. OSC; acknowledgment by AFL)
No statutory entitlement alleged to § 1214-style notices in a § 1216 investigation; therefore no concrete informational injury
Redressability: even if court ordered an investigation under § 1216, OSC retains discretion whether to provide § 1214 notices; relief would not be reasonably likely to yield the sought information

Disposition and significance: D.C. Circuit vacates and remands with instructions to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction; takeaways on limits of procedural and informational standing when statutory entitlements and non-party discretion are absent
